blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Language-conditioned traffic simulation enables scalable test scenarios steered by natural language. The goal is to control selected agents while surrounding traffic reacts to their observed behaviour. For example, a vehicle instructed to cut in late should cause the following vehicle to brake only when the manoeuvre becomes observable. Yet simulators can leak private instructions across agents, causing surrounding vehicles to react before the instructed behaviour becomes observable. Such premature reactions defuse desired events and alter the ensuing closed-loop scenario. Existing benchmarks measure what agents do, not what they could have known, leaving this failure unmeasured. We formalise it as intent leakage and address it through evaluation, data and modelling. Our paired intervention test holds an instructed agent's executed trajectory fixed while varying its private instruction, isolating leakage-induced changes in surrounding agents. We also construct WOMD-PACT, an automatically generated, verifiable dataset of 531,099 WOMD scenes with timed behaviour tags with reaction episodes identified through a counterfactual ghost test and grounded private instructions. Finally, we introduce CaFe, a dual-stream diffusion-forcing simulator fine-tuned in closed loop that restricts inter-agent interactions to public beliefs, preserving legitimate anticipation without leaking private intent. Our evaluation reveals that existing conditioning designs displace 23-83% of nearby uninstructed agents through private-intent leakage, even when the instructed agent's executed motion is held fixed. CaFe eliminates measurable leakage while maintaining comparable WOSAC realism (0.763), demonstrating that causal faithfulness can be enforced without sacrificing measured simulation realism.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en: The validation of autonomous vehicles (AVs) requires, among many other aspects, exposing the system to safety-critical interactions, such as aggressive cut-ins or failures to yield, which occur rarely in logged driving data. Traffic simulation addresses this scarcity by reproducing such interactions on demand. Rule-based simulators and scenario description languages [ 2 , 10 , 13 ] offer precise control but require scenarios to be authored by hand, whereas data-driven simulators [ 36 , 45 , 42 , 17 ] learn realistic behaviour from logged driving yet provide little control over which interactions arise. Conditional generation reconciles the two by steering a learned behaviour model with goal positions [ 48 , 49 ] , behaviour tags [ 37 ] or natural language [ 38 , 47 , 37 , 43 , 4 ] . Instructions are typically given to a subset of agents, while the others respond based on what they observe. For instance, one vehicle may be instructed to cut in ahead of another, leaving the response of surrounding traffic to the simulator.

blocks.en: This expectation does not hold in current simulators. ProSim [ 37 ] conditions each agent’s policy on the text of the entire scene, while LangTraj [ 4 ] additionally lets agents attend to the text-conditioned future trajectories of others. We term this exposure intent leakage . Its visible consequence is a preemptive reaction , where an uninstructed agent responds to an intention before any motion expresses it. In the example above, the surrounding vehicle decelerates before the instructed vehicle begins its cut-in ( ). The conflict is thereby resolved in advance, and the premature response propagates through the closed-loop rollout.

blocks.en:
We formalise intent leakage as any influence of an instruction
on another agent that does not pass through
the instructed agent’s observable motion. This extends interventional
evaluation of interactive prediction to private instructions
held by any agent. Measuring leakage requires separating it from legitimate reaction, since removing an instruction also changes the instructed agent’s motion, to which others may rightly respond. We therefore compare paired closed-loop rollouts with shared random seeds, replaying the instructed agents’ generated trajectories with and without their instructions. The uninstructed agents observe identical instructed-agent motion in both runs, so any difference in their responses reveals leakage, while a simulator without leakage yields exactly zero.

blocks.en: Preventing leakage requires care in both the data and the model. An instruction that describes another agent’s intended behaviour reveals its plan before that behaviour becomes observable. Existing language datasets often describe a reaction together with its cause [ 37 , 4 ] . WOMD-PACT therefore derives private instructions from measured behaviour. Timed behaviour tags record what each road user does and when, while a counterfactual ghost test identifies the likely causes of reactions. At evaluation, reacting agents receive no instruction and must respond to observed motion.

blocks.en:
Training and evaluation require four data properties: verifiable facts , private instructions , symmetric coverage across vehicles, and reaction annotations for selective prompting.
While the replay test reports leakage through models, instruction
privacy must be ensured during data construction.
ProSim-Instruct-520k and InterDrive include
scene-level or cross-agent descriptions in single-sentence instructions [ 37 , 4 ] ,
which can expose information beyond a recipient’s observed history.
WOMD-PACT instead derives private instructions from measured behaviour
on all 531,099 WOMD training and validation
scenes [ 11 ] , each spanning 9.1 s at 10 Hz.
It comprises timed behaviour tags, an interaction graph and private
language instructions.

blocks.en: 7 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 7 结论

blocks.en:
We formalize intent leakage and introduce a paired replay test
that separates it from legitimate reactions to observed motion.
WOMD-PACT addresses privacy in instruction construction, while
CaFe enforces it in inter-agent information flow.
Our results show that eliminating measured leakage is compatible
with comparable realism, instruction following and response
quality. This establishes the feasibility of causally faithful
conditional simulation and motivates stronger leak-free
simulators. Extending this principle across conditioning modalities
would broaden its use in controllable scenario generation.

具有可比较的现实主义、后续指示和反应

blocks.en:
Limitations. Our evaluation focuses on language conditioning. The same
information boundary can be formulated for goal points, route
sketches and other private conditions, but these extensions
remain untested. CaFe demonstrates one practical implementation
using a frozen backbone to form public beliefs. More elaborate
belief representations and conditioning mechanisms remain to be
explored, offering scope to improve generation quality while
preserving causal faithfulness.
